name: Liraglutide

track.title: Lab & animal
track.line: Rat and mouse studies, incl. thyroid C-cell tumors

track.title: Generics
track.line: Generics since Dec 2024; on FDA shortage list

what.text: Liraglutide is a man-made version of GLP-1, a hormone the gut releases after eating. The Saxenda label says it shares 97% of its sequence with human GLP-1. A fatty acid is attached so it lasts longer in the body: its half-life is about 13 hours, so it is injected once a day. It switches on the GLP-1 receptor, and the label says it lowers body weight by lowering how many calories people eat. It does not raise the energy the body burns over 24 hours.
In animal studies, liraglutide reached brain areas that control appetite, including the hypothalamus. That finding comes from animals.

The FDA-approved brands are Victoza, for type 2 diabetes, and Saxenda, for weight management. Both are made by Novo Nordisk and given by injection under the skin. Xultophy combines liraglutide with insulin degludec. FDA has also approved generic liraglutide.

research.text: Liraglutide has been tested in large randomized trials paid for by its maker, Novo Nordisk. Two are listed below as they were run: the main weight trial behind Saxenda and the heart-outcome trial behind Victoza’s heart use.

research.title: SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes: weight in adults without diabetes

facts.v: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled. Two people got liraglutide for every one on placebo.
3,731 adults with a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with treated or untreated high blood fats or high blood pressure. None had type 2 diabetes; 61.2% had prediabetes. 78.5% were women.
a daily 3.0 mg liraglutide injection or placebo, both with lifestyle counseling
change in body weight, and how many people lost at least 5% and more than 10%

research.found: At 56 weeks, people on liraglutide had lost an average of 8.4 kg and people on placebo 2.8 kg. 63.2% on liraglutide and 27.1% on placebo lost at least 5% of their weight; 33.1% and 10.6% lost more than 10%. Nausea and diarrhea were the most common side effects. Serious events happened in 6.2% on liraglutide and 5.0% on placebo. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01272219.

src.label: Pi-Sunyer et al., SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes, N Engl J Med
SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes trial record, ClinicalTrials.gov

research.title: LEADER: heart outcomes in type 2 diabetes

facts.v: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled. Built first to show liraglutide did not raise heart risk.
9,340 adults with type 2 diabetes and high heart risk
liraglutide (1.8 mg in the label’s description) or placebo, on top of standard care
first heart-related death, non-fatal heart attack or non-fatal stroke, counted together

research.found: The combined outcome happened in 13.0% on liraglutide and 14.9% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.87). Heart-related deaths were 4.7% and 6.0%. Stomach and bowel effects were the most common reason people stopped liraglutide. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01179048.

src.label: Marso et al., LEADER, N Engl J Med

research.text: The Saxenda label describes two more 56-week weight trials: one in 635 adults with type 2 diabetes, where average weight changed by -5.4% on Saxenda and -1.7% on placebo, and one in 422 adults who had first lost at least 5% on a low-calorie diet, where weight changed by a further -4.9% on Saxenda and +0.3% on placebo. In the 56-week trials, about 10% on Saxenda and 4% on placebo stopped because of side effects.
In rats and mice, liraglutide caused thyroid C-cell tumors, including cancers, at exposures similar to those in people. This is the basis of the boxed warning below.

us.text: Liraglutide is FDA approved as Victoza (type 2 diabetes, 2010) and Saxenda (weight management, 2014), and as generics. FDA’s shortage records still list liraglutide injection as in shortage. Compounded liraglutide is not FDA approved. As of November 1, 2026.
Compounded drugs are not FDA approved. FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness or quality before they are sold.

src.label: FDA, Compounding and the FDA: Q&A

items.text: approved, with diet and exercise, to improve blood sugar control in adults and children 10 and older with type 2 diabetes, and to lower the risk of major heart events in adults with type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

approved, with a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity, to reduce excess weight and keep it off in adults with obesity, adults with overweight and at least one weight-related condition, and children 12 and older who weigh more than 60 kg and have obesity.
FDA records list generic liraglutide approved since December 2024. Some generic labels match Victoza’s diabetes uses; others match Saxenda’s weight use.

Victoza is approved for type 2 diabetes, not for weight management. Using it for weight loss is off-label. The Saxenda label says the benefit of liraglutide below 3 mg a day for weight reduction has not been established.

FDA’s shortage records list liraglutide injection as a current shortage, first posted July 18, 2023. In September 2026 updates, Victoza and Saxenda pens were listed as having limited availability, and some generic versions as available.

world.lead: Liraglutide is an approved, prescription medicine in the US, Canada, the UK, the EU and Australia. Which brand is approved for which use differs by country. It is not prohibited in sport.

countries.status: Approved medicine (Victoza for type 2 diabetes; Saxenda for weight management; generics). Prescription-only. Compounded versions are not FDA approved.

after.title: Sport
after.text: The WADA 2026 Prohibited List does not name liraglutide or GLP-1 drugs. USADA says GLP-1 medicines are not prohibited in sport and need no therapeutic use exemption. WADA’s 2027 Monitoring Program, which tracks use without banning, names only semaglutide and tirzepatide among GLP-1 drugs.

src.label: USADA: Weight loss drugs, what athletes need to know about GLP-1s

side.text: Every liraglutide label has a boxed warning, FDA’s strongest kind, about thyroid C-cell tumors. The most common side effects are stomach and bowel effects. The labels list other serious risks, below.

items.text: in rats and mice, liraglutide caused thyroid C-cell tumors. It is not known if it causes them in people. Cases of medullary thyroid cancer have been reported in people using liraglutide since approval, but the label says the reports cannot show whether liraglutide caused them. People with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer, or with MEN 2 syndrome, must not use it.
inflammation of the pancreas, including fatal and bleeding or dead-tissue forms, has been seen with GLP-1 medicines including liraglutide.
in Saxenda trials, gallstones were reported in 2.2% on Saxenda and 0.8% on placebo, and gallbladder inflammation in 0.8% and 0.4%. Most people with these events needed gallbladder surgery.
resting heart rate rose by an average of 2 to 3 beats per minute compared with placebo.
there are reports of sudden kidney injury, some needing dialysis, mostly in people who became dehydrated from nausea, vomiting or diarrhea.
reported in 4.8% on Saxenda and 1.4% on placebo in trials.
the risk is higher when liraglutide is used with insulin or drugs that raise insulin release.
serious reactions, including anaphylaxis and swelling under the skin (angioedema), have been reported.
liraglutide slows stomach emptying. There are rare reports of stomach contents entering the lungs during general anesthesia or deep sedation.
the Saxenda label says weight loss offers no benefit in pregnancy and may harm the fetus, and to stop Saxenda when pregnancy is recognized.
nausea, diarrhea, constipation, vomiting, injection site reactions, headache, low blood sugar, indigestion, tiredness, dizziness, belly pain, raised lipase, fever and stomach flu.
the February 2026 Saxenda label removed its warning section on suicidal behavior and ideation.

surprises: FDA’s shortage records still list liraglutide injection as a current shortage in October 2026, unlike semaglutide and tirzepatide, whose shortages FDA declared resolved.
The maker plans to stop Saxenda in January 2027, according to FDA’s shortage record, while generic weight-management liraglutide is FDA approved.
The Saxenda label removed its warning on suicidal behavior and ideation in February 2026.
